message.content:
### Your Rights as a Tenant in Texas (as of 2026) | Area | What You’re Entitled To | How to Exercise It | |------|------------------------|--------------------| | **Security Deposit** | • The landlord may hold a maximum of **one month’s rent** (or two if the lease is for a furnished unit).
• The deposit must be returned within **30 days** after you move out, minus any lawful deductions. | • Keep a copy of the lease and any move‑in inspection report.
• Request a written itemized statement of deductions if the landlord withholds part of the deposit. | | **Habitability** | • The landlord must keep the premises in a **safe, sanitary, and livable condition** (e.g., functioning plumbing, heating, electrical, pest control). | • Notify the landlord in writing (email or certified mail) of any needed repairs.
• If repairs are not made within a reasonable time, you may:
 • Withhold rent (but only after giving notice and following the proper procedure).
 • Pay for the repair yourself and deduct the cost from your rent (Texas Property Code §92.006). | | **Rent Payment** | • Rent is due on the date specified in the lease.
• Late fees are allowed only if the lease states them and they are **reasonable** (not punitive). | • Keep receipts or bank records of payments.
• If you’re late, notify the landlord and ask for a grace period if possible. | | **Lease Termination** | • **Month‑to‑month** tenants can terminate with **30 days’ written notice**.
• Tenants who signed a fixed‑term lease can terminate early only if the lease allows it or if the landlord breaches the lease. | • Provide written notice (email or certified mail) and keep a copy. | | **Right to Privacy** | • Landlords may enter only for **reasonable reasons** (repairs, inspections, showing the unit to prospective buyers/renters).
• They must give **at least 24 hours’ written notice** (unless it’s an emergency). | • Keep a log of any entries.
• If the landlord enters without notice, you can file a complaint with the Texas Attorney General’s Office. | | **Discrimination** | • Landlords cannot discriminate based on **race, color, religion, sex, national origin, familial status, disability, or source of income** (including public assistance). | • File a complaint with the Texas Commission on Human Rights or the U.S. Department of Housing and Urban Development (HUD). | | **Security Deposit Deductions** | • Deductions must be for **actual damages** beyond normal wear and tear. | • Request an itemized list. If you disagree, you can file a claim in small claims court (up to $20,000). | | **Repair and Deduct** | • If the landlord fails to repair a habitability issue within a reasonable time, you may pay for the repair and deduct the cost from your rent. | • Keep receipts and provide the landlord with a written notice of the deduction. | | **Eviction Process** | • The landlord must follow the **Texas Property Code** eviction procedures: serve a written notice (e.g., 3‑day notice for nonpayment, 30‑day notice for lease termination).
• The landlord cannot evict you without a court order. | • Respond to notices promptly.
• If you receive an eviction notice, you can file a **motion to dismiss** or a **motion for summary judgment** in the county court. | | **Rent Control & Rent Increase** | • Texas has **no statewide rent control**. Landlords can increase rent at the end of a lease term or with proper notice (usually 30 days for month‑to‑month). | • Review your lease for any rent‑increase clauses. | | **Utilities** | • The lease should specify which utilities you are responsible for. | • Verify the lease and keep records of utility payments. | | **Subletting & Assignment** | • Many leases allow subletting or assignment with landlord’s written consent. | • Obtain written permission before subletting. | | **Legal Assistance** | • **Texas Attorney General’s Office**: Consumer Protection Division.
• **Local tenant‑rights groups** and **legal aid clinics**. | • Contact them for free or low‑cost legal advice. | --- #### Quick Checklist for Tenants 1. **Read Your Lease** – Understand all terms, especially regarding rent, deposits, repairs, and notice periods. 2. **Document Everything** – Keep copies of all communications, receipts, and inspection reports. 3. **Know the Notice Requirements** – 24‑hour notice for entry, 30‑day notice for termination, etc. 4. **Respond Promptly** – If you receive a notice (rent increase, eviction, repair request), reply in writing and keep a copy. 5. **Seek Legal Help Early** – If you suspect a violation, contact a tenant‑rights organization or attorney before the situation escalates. --- #### Resources | Resource | What It Offers | How to Access | |----------|----------------|---------------| | **Texas Attorney General – Consumer Protection** | Free legal advice, complaint filing, consumer guides. | https://www.texasattorneygeneral.gov/consumer-protection | | **Texas Commission on Human Rights** | Complaint filing for discrimination. | https://www.tchrc.org/ | | **HUD – Fair Housing** | National resources, complaint filing. | https://www.hud.gov/ | | **Local Legal Aid Clinics** | Free or low‑cost representation. | Search “legal aid Texas” + your city. | | **Texas Property Code** | Official statutory text. | https://statutes.capitol.texas.gov/ | --- ### Bottom Line As a Texas tenant, you have the right to a safe, habitable home, fair treatment regarding deposits and rent, privacy, and protection against discrimination. If a landlord violates these rights, you can take legal action—often starting with a written notice, then possibly filing a claim in small claims court or a lawsuit in county court. Always keep thorough records and seek professional help if you’re unsure how to proceed.
